source.title: Gated Convolutional Networks with Hybrid Connectivity for Image Classification
source.authors: Chuan-Guang Yang; Zhu-Lin An; Hui Zhu; Xiaolong Hu; Kun Zhang; Kaiqiang Xu; Chao Li; Bo-Yu Diao; Yong-Jun Xu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares CNN interpretability using network dissection, a different measure from the claim’s pole-level job explanations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a network-dissection comparison of ImageNet-pretrained vision models. It does not measure neuron-pole job shares, explanations tested on held-out activations, language models, or any of the other claim versions’ named outcomes. The network-dissection result is retained as evidence relevant to V4’s vision-model interpretability comparison; it is not a measurement of the claimed share of interpretable neurons.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper (HCGNet). It uses network dissection only to score its own model against other ImageNet CNNs, as one of several selling points alongside accuracy and robustness. It does not measure the share of neurons with one main job. It does not test whether architecture, regularization or tools cause interpretability. It does not address any language-model, polysemanticity, circuit or explanation-scoring version. The result is the study's own method compared with others, so it is not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors say HCGNet-B obtains the highest network-dissection score with least complexity. They present this as evidence that hybrid connectivity and SMG modules give better latent representations, alongside accuracy, robustness and transfer gains.
record.recipe_differences: Uses network dissection to count unique detectors in a CNN’s final convolutional layer, rather than explaining neuron poles and testing explanations on held-out activations.

fits_no_version.finding: Network dissection on the final conv layer of ImageNet-pretrained CNNs. HCGNet-B reportedly has the highest number of unique concept detectors among about 20 models, including GoogLeNet, ResNets and DenseNets (Figure 4, values not in text).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unique-detector counts from network dissection differ across CNN architectures, and newer architectures can yield more unique detectors in the final layer.

record.problems: The reported interpretability result is a network-dissection detector count, not a percentage of neurons with a single job. The text gives no numerical score or uncertainty for Figure 4.
record.rows_left_out: No other outcomes bearing on the claim versions were reported as text or assignable numerical results. Figure 4 plots detector counts for comparison models, but the provided text does not state their individual values.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B pole shares (about 90% one job, about 7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood).
Shares in other language models, dense and MoE, at any scale.
InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, pose feature, recursive generalization vs superposition.
Share of interpretable neurons. Causal role of architecture, regularization and tools. The InceptionV1-sized estimates from about 5% to about 99%.
Neuron-based attribution graphs and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict firing.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' and its 'supports V4' label should be dropped. The unique-detector count is not a share of interpretable neurons. The comparison only promotes the authors' own architecture, with no analysis of why. Figure 4's per-model counts (including GoogLeNet/InceptionV1) are only in the plot, not the extracted text. Even if read off the plot, they are counts of unique concepts, not interpretable-unit fractions.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level shares of single-job, related-job, and not-yet-understood poles.
Language-model results across model sizes, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
The percentage of interpretable neurons or poles; the cited estimates for InceptionV1-sized models; effects of regularization and tools; and whether architecture causes the difference.
Attribution graphs built from a model’s own neurons and their reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples predict firing on new activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: HCGNet-B
rows.operation_detail: Network dissection comparing the number of unique detectors in the final convolutional layer.
rows.measure: Number of unique detectors (network dissection interpretability score)
rows.value: Overall highest score among the compared models, with least complexity.
rows.note: The text gives this comparative conclusion but no numerical detector count. This measure does not quantify the share of neurons with one main job.
rows.check: This row compares the study's own model against other models, not a measurement of the claim. The measure is a count of unique detectors in the final conv layer, not a share of interpretable neurons. No numbers are stated in the text, and no baseline is given. A single new architecture topping a leaderboard cannot show that modern architectures or better tools raise interpretable-neuron shares. The 'observed' state should be cannot_determine.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: HCGNet-B is reported to obtain the overall highest interpretability score with least complexity; this supports the architecture-comparison aspect of V4, but does not measure its claimed interpretable-neuron share (R1).
